{{nihongo|'''Chikushi Shrine'''|筑紫神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Chikuzen Province]].

'''Chikushi Shrine''' (ちくしじんじゃ / つくしじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258|qid=Q123258}}{{ill|Chikushino, Fukuoka|ar|تشيكوشينو (فوكوكا)|azb|چیکوشینو، فوکوئوکا|ce|Тикусино|ceb|Chikushino-shi (lungsod)|de|Chikushino|eo|Ĉikuŝino|es|Chikushino (Fukuoka)|fa|چیکوشینو، فوکوئوکا|fi|Chikushino|fr|Chikushino|gl|Chikushino|hak|Chikushino, Fukuoka|it|Chikushino|ja|筑紫野市|ko|지쿠시노시|mg|Chikushino-shi|mzn|چیکوشینو، فوکوئوکا|nl|Chikushino|no|Chikushino|pl|Chikushino|pt|Chikushino|ro|Chikushino|ru|Тикусино|sv|Chikushino|tg|Чикушино|tl|Chikushino, Fukuoka|tr|Chikushino|tt|Тикусино|uk|Чікушіно|ur|چیکوشینو، فوکوکا|vi|Chikushino, Fukuoka|war|Chikushino, Fukuoka|zh|筑紫野市|zh_classical|筑紫野市|zh_min_nan|Tikusino-chhī|zh_yue|筑紫野|qid=Q844140}}{{ill|Harada|ja|原田 (筑紫野市)|qid=Q11409733|lt=Harada}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}), and under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=former shrine ranking}} it was a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural Shrine}}.

=== Enshrined deities ===
The current enshrined deities are the following three kami<ref>The list of deities is based on the shrine’s official history.</ref>.
* '''Chikushi no Kami''' (つくしのかみ) – the {{ill|Kunitama|fr|Kunitama|ja|国魂|simple|Kunitama|zh|國魂|qid=Q9692242}} (tutelary spirit) of {{ill|Tsukushi Province|de|Provinz Tsukushi|fa|ولایت تسوکوشی|ff|Tsukushi Province|fr|Province de Tsukushi|it|Tsukushi (provincia)|ja|筑紫国|ko|쓰쿠시국|nl|Tsukushi (provincie)|simple|Tsukushi Province|th|แคว้นสึกูชิ|zh|筑紫國|zh_min_nan|Tukusi-kok|qid=Q1206461|lt=Chikushi}}.
* {{ill|Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|Q3082751|qid=Q3082751|lt=Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto}} – later invited from {{ill|Kamado Shrine|fr|Kamado-jinja|ja|竈門神社|simple|Kamado Shrine|zh|竈門神社|qid=Q11597744}}.
* {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|Q941979|qid=Q941979}} – later enshrined together (gōshi).

=== About the enshrined deities ===
An excerpt from the *Chikugo no Kuni Fudoki*, quoted in the {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|Q2710483|qid=Q2710483}}, states that {{ill|Chikugo Province|cs|Provincie Čikugo|de|Provinz Chikugo|eo|Provinco Ĉikugo|es|Provincia de Chikugo|fa|ولایت چیکوگو|fi|Chikugon provinssi|fr|Province de Chikugo|gl|Provincia de Chikugo|id|Provinsi Chikugo|it|Chikugo (provincia)|ja|筑後国|ko|지쿠고국|lt|Čikugo žemė|nl|Chikugo (provincie)|pt|Província de Chikugo|ru|Тикуго (провинция)|simple|Chikugo Province|sk|Čikugo (provincia)|sr|Провинција Чикуго|tr|Chikugo (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тікуґо|zh|筑後國|zh_min_nan|Tikugo-kok|zh_yue|筑後國|qid=Q864159}} was originally one province together with {{ill|Chikuzen Province|cs|Provincie Čikuzen|de|Provinz Chikuzen|es|Provincia de Chikuzen|fa|ولایت چیکوزن|fr|Chikuzen|gl|Provincia de Chikuzen|id|Provinsi Chikuzen|it|Chikuzen (provincia)|ja|筑前国|ko|지쿠젠국|lt|Čikudzeno žemė|nl|Chikuzen (provincie)|no|Chikuzen (provins)|pt|Província de Chikuzen|ru|Тикудзэн (провинция)|simple|Chikuzen Province|sk|Čikuzen (provincia)|sr|Провинција Чикузен|tr|Chikuzen (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тікудзен|zh|筑前國|zh_min_nan|Tikuzen-kok|zh_yue|筑前國|qid=Q1047664}}, forming {{ill|Tsukushi Province|de|Provinz Tsukushi|fa|ولایت تسوکوشی|ff|Tsukushi Province|fr|Province de Tsukushi|it|Tsukushi (provincia)|ja|筑紫国|ko|쓰쿠시국|nl|Tsukushi (provincie)|simple|Tsukushi Province|th|แคว้นสึกูชิ|zh|筑紫國|zh_min_nan|Tukusi-kok|qid=Q1206461}}. As for the origin of the name “Chikushi,” three theories are recorded: (1) the mountain pass between the two provinces was so steep that saddles were worn out, hence “kurazukushi” (“saddles exhausted”); (2) a violent deity dwelled at the border of the two provinces, causing travelers to lose their lives—thus “inochi-zukushi” (“lives exhausted”)—until the deity was pacified through the rites of the Chikushi no Kimi and Higo no Kimi; and (3) to mourn the many deaths in the previous theory, coffins were made and the mountains were stripped of trees, giving rise to “kizukushi” (“trees exhausted”). Among these, a connection between the second theory and Chikushi Shrine’s enshrined deity, Chikushi no Kami, has been pointed out. {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|Q384647|qid=Q384647}} regarded the “inochi-zukushi” theory as the most plausible in his {{ill|Kojiki-den|Q11410835|qid=Q11410835}}. Although it is unclear whether these legends are directly related to the founding of Chikushi Shrine, particular attention is paid to the tradition that the shrine was worshipped by the Chikushi no Kimi ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Chikushi no Kuni no Miyatsuko}}) and the Higo no Kimi ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hi no Kuni no Miyatsuko}})<ref name="神々"/>. While this area lay within the sphere of influence of the Chikushi no Kimi, the advance of the Higo no Kimi from central Kyushu to northern Kyushu was triggered by the {{ill|Iwai Rebellion|Q3138004|qid=Q3138004}} in the mid-6th century, and this tradition is considered to reflect ritual relations after that advance<ref name="神々"/>. Furthermore, from the theory that Shirahiwake no Kami and {{ill|Isotakeru-no-Mikoto|qid=Q10881556|lt=Isotakeru-no-Mikoto}} were the ancestral deities of the Chikushi and Higo provincial rulers, it is assumed that the {{ill|Chikushi clan|Q11602927|qid=Q11602927}} of the {{ill|Shōni clan|Q2975368|qid=Q2975368}} lineage, which later served Chikushi Shrine, succeeded the position of the Chikushi no Kimi, descendants of the provincial governors<ref>{{ill|Toshio Hōga|Q11452691|qid=Q11452691}} “6. Early sections of the Okinaga-related clans,” *Studies on Ancient Clans ⑥: The Okinaga Clan—A Smithing Clan that Produced Great Kings*, Aogaki Publishing, 2014, pp. 123–124.</ref>.

In addition, there are theories identifying Chikushi no Kami as Shirahiwake no Kami or as {{ill|Isotakeru-no-Mikoto|qid=Q10881556|lt=Isotakeru-no-Mikoto}}<ref name="由緒書"/>.
* Shirahiwake no Kami theory  
*: Proposed by Yoshimura Chiharu<ref name="由緒書"/>. In the {{ill|Kojiki|Q813031|qid=Q813031}} {{ill|Kuniumi|es|Mito de la creación de Japón|eu|Kuniumi|fa|کونیئومی|fr|Kuniumi|it|Kuniumi|ja|国産み|pl|Kuniumi|ru|Куниуми|th|คูนิอูมิ|tl|Kuniumi|zh|国诞生|qid=Q3545163|lt=creation myth}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tsukushi Island}} (Kyushu) is described as having four faces: {{ill|Tsukushi Province|de|Provinz Tsukushi|fa|ولایت تسوکوشی|ff|Tsukushi Province|fr|Province de Tsukushi|it|Tsukushi (provincia)|ja|筑紫国|ko|쓰쿠시국|nl|Tsukushi (provincie)|simple|Tsukushi Province|th|แคว้นสึกูชิ|zh|筑紫國|zh_min_nan|Tukusi-kok|qid=Q1206461}}, {{ill|Toyo Province|Q1205043|qid=Q1205043}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Higo Province}}, and {{ill|Kumaso|Q1196897|qid=Q1196897|lt=Kumaso Province}}, and it is stated that “Chikushi Province is called Shirahiwake.” Since the Chinese character “白” (white) was used as a phonetic loan in Korea to represent light, brightness, or the sun, a connection with Korea has been suggested<ref name="神々">*Gods of Japan*, entry on Chikushi Shrine.</ref>.
* Isotakeru-no-Mikoto theory  
*: Proposed by Matsushita Kenrin and {{ill|Toshio Hōga|Q11452691|qid=Q11452691|lt=Kaibara Ekiken}}<ref name="由緒書"/>. In an alternative divine-age tradition in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935}}, {{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Q272993|qid=Q272993}} descends to Silla accompanied by Isotakeru-no-Kami (Isotakeru-no-Mikoto), later moving to Izumo. Isotakeru-no-Kami is said to have possessed many kinds of trees, but did not plant them in Korea, instead sowing them throughout the country beginning in Chikushi. From these legends, Isotakeru-no-Kami is thought to have been a deity of immigrant origin, again suggesting a connection with Korea<ref name="神々"/>.

=== History ===
=== Founding ===
The date of founding is unknown. There are theories that the shrine was originally worshipped on the summit of Mount Shiroyama and later moved to the foothills, or that it was enshrined at the current location from the beginning<ref>Relocation theory: *Zoku Fudoki Shūi*; non-relocation theory: *Zoku Fudoki* (both cited in *Place Names of Fukuoka Prefecture*, entry on Chikushi Shrine).</ref>.

The name “Chikushi” in a broad sense referred to the whole of Kyushu, as in “Chikushi Island” ({{ill|Kojiki|Q813031|qid=Q813031}}) or “Chikushi Province” ({{ill|Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935}}), but in a narrower sense it is said to refer to the place name around Chikushi Shrine<ref name="神々"/>. Archaeologically, the low hilly area on the eastern side of the Sefuri Mountains around this site was a central area for jar-coffin burials in the Middle Yayoi period, and for bronze production in the Late Yayoi period<ref name="神々"/>. The origins of dōtaku (bronze bell) rituals are also thought to lie in this region, and their flourishing would have required immigrant knowledge; taken together with the traditions of Shirahiwake and Isotakeru-no-Mikoto, ritual practices by immigrant groups have been suggested<ref name="神々"/>.

=== Outline history ===
The earliest mention in the {{ill|Rikkokushi|Q1151168|qid=Q1151168|lt=official histories}} records that in the first year of {{ill|Jōgan|Q1075635|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} ({{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}}) the shrine received the divine rank of Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade, and in the third year of {{ill|Gangyō|Q747451|qid=Q747451}} ({{ill|879|Q25001|qid=Q25001}}) it was promoted to Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade.

In the *{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}* (compiled in {{ill|927|Q30470|qid=Q30470}}), within the *{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=Register of Shrines}}*, it is listed under {{ill|Mikasa district|ja|御笠郡|pl|Powiat Mikasa|zh|御笠郡|qid=Q11071211}} of {{ill|Chikuzen Province|cs|Provincie Čikuzen|de|Provinz Chikuzen|es|Provincia de Chikuzen|fa|ولایت چیکوزن|fr|Chikuzen|gl|Provincia de Chikuzen|id|Provinsi Chikuzen|it|Chikuzen (provincia)|ja|筑前国|ko|지쿠젠국|lt|Čikudzeno žemė|nl|Chikuzen (provincie)|no|Chikuzen (provins)|pt|Província de Chikuzen|ru|Тикудзэн (провинция)|simple|Chikuzen Province|sk|Čikuzen (provincia)|sr|Провинција Чикузен|tr|Chikuzen (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Тікудзен|zh|筑前國|zh_min_nan|Tikuzen-kok|zh_yue|筑前國|qid=Q1047664}} as “Chikushi Shrine, Myōjin Taisha,” placing it among the {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}. A government order from the second year of {{ill|Tengen (era)|Q1327101|qid=Q1327101|lt=Tengen}} ({{ill|979|Q23784|qid=Q23784}}) records that a chief priest (daigūji) post was established at Chikushi Shrine along with {{ill|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)|Q29682|qid=Q29682|lt=Sumiyoshi Shrine}}, {{ill|Kashii-gū|Q631373|qid=Q631373}}, {{ill|Kamado Shrine|fr|Kamado-jinja|ja|竈門神社|simple|Kamado Shrine|zh|竈門神社|qid=Q11597744}}, and {{ill|Hakozaki Shrine|Q714742|qid=Q714742}}<ref name="由緒書"/>.

From the {{ill|Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205}}, the {{ill|Chikushi clan|Q11602927|qid=Q11602927}}, who served as local stewards (jitō), also served as shrine priests<ref name="由緒書"/>. Later, during the {{ill|Sengoku period|Q204023|qid=Q204023|lt=Warring States period}}, the shrine buildings and ancient documents were burned in warfare by the forces of the {{ill|Shimazu clan|Q1061406|qid=Q1061406}}, and the shrine fell into ruin due to bandit attacks<ref name="由緒書"/>. In the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963}}, restoration efforts were undertaken and the shrine buildings were rebuilt<ref name="由緒書"/>.

After the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|Q8707|qid=Q8707}}, in the fifth year of {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} ({{ill|1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753}}) the shrine was ranked as a {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}} under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern shrine ranking system}}, but became a {{ill|Son-sha|Q134917284|qid=Q134917284}} following administrative reforms. In Meiji 14 ({{ill|1881|Q7808|qid=Q7808}}) it was again promoted to Gōsha, and in the fourth year of {{ill|Taishō era|Q329174|qid=Q329174}} ({{ill|1915|Q2084|qid=Q2084}}) it was elevated to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural Shrine}}<ref name="由緒書">Shrine official history.</ref>.

=== Festivals ===
=== Annual festivals ===
* New Year Festival (January 1–3)<ref>Festival information is based on the shrine’s official history.</ref>
* {{ill|Kayu ura|Q11604655|qid=Q11604655|lt=Kayūra Festival}} (also called Okayu-ura Festival; Spring Grand Festival) (March 15)
* Oyodo (summer festival), Summer purification rite (July 19)
* Annual Festival (Autumn Grand Festival) (October 20)

=== Kayūra Festival ===
The '''Kayūra Festival''' (かゆうらさい) is held every year on March 15, commonly known as “'''Kayūra'''.” It is a divination ritual that predicts the year’s harvest and outbreaks of disease by observing the {{ill|Mold|Q159341|qid=Q159341}} that grows on {{ill|Congee|Q878624|qid=Q878624|lt=okayu}}.

On February 15, water drawn from the shrine’s {{ill|Well|Q43483|qid=Q43483}} is used by the shrine priest to cook rice porridge over a {{ill|Temple|Q44539|qid=Q44539|lt=kamado}}. The porridge is then placed in a large {{ill|Hachi|Q56351193|qid=Q56351193}}, and {{ill|Chopsticks|Q81980|qid=Q81980}} are laid in a cross on top. The center of the cross represents Chikushi Shrine, and name tags representing areas to the east, west, south, and north as seen from the shrine are inserted into the porridge. The porridge is then placed in the shrine’s {{ill|Temple|Q44539|qid=Q44539}} for one month. On March 15, the day of the Kayūra Festival, the priest removes the porridge and judges the condition of the mold on its surface to determine the year’s {{ill|Cereal|Q12117|qid=Q12117}} harvest and whether {{ill|Contagious disease|Q2995419|qid=Q2995419}} will spread. The judgments are made according to an ancient Kayūra divination manual preserved by the shrine, and the results are posted at the shrine.

This Kayūra Festival has been designated an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Chikushino City<ref name="筑紫野市">[http://www.city.chikushino.fukuoka.jp/kyouikubu/bunka-joho/tikusizinnzyakayuura.html Chikushi Shrine Kayūra Divination Ritual and Porridge Bowl] (Chikushino City website).</ref>.
